name: Faro
description: Faro is an iconic 19th-century banking game immortalized in American frontier lore as the favorite of gamblers like Wyatt Earp and Doc Holliday. Known colloquially as 'Bucking the Tiger' (from the tiger illustrations on dealing boxes), it is a game of pure chance where players wager on which card ranks will be drawn from a specially-designed dealing box. Unlike poker, Faro was prized for its transparency and relatively low house edge, allowing players to track all remaining cards using a public tool called a 'Case Keeper'.

overview.description: Faro is an iconic 19th-century banking game immortalized in American frontier lore as the favorite of gamblers like Wyatt Earp and Doc Holliday. Known colloquially as 'Bucking the Tiger' (from the tiger illustrations on dealing boxes), it is a game of pure chance where players wager on which card ranks will be drawn from a specially-designed dealing box. Unlike poker, Faro was prized for its transparency and relatively low house edge, allowing players to track all remaining cards using a public tool called a 'Case Keeper'.

history.origins: Faro descended from the French game Pharaon (1688), which itself derived from the Italian game Bassetta introduced to Paris in the early 17th century. Introduced to the USA via New Orleans, it spread rapidly across the frontier during the 19th century.
timeline: 1688: Pharaon documented in France, becomes popular in royal courts.
1710: Faro emerges as the preferred English name; dominates European gambling salons.
1840-1890: Golden Age of Faro in the American Wild West; present in nearly every gambling hall and saloon.
1915: Game begins decline in the USA due to increased regulation and cheating concerns.
1955: Last permanent Faro bank in Nevada closes; game becomes historical curiosity.
Present: Played occasionally at Western reenactments and historical gambling demonstrations.
history.cultural: Faro is a recurring motif in American literature (Mark Twain, Bret Harte) and Western cinema, representing frontier democracy, high stakes, and the gambler's code. The phrase 'Bucking the Tiger' became synonymous with taking a risk.
history.evolution: The game evolved from a high-house-edge French social game into a strictly regulated casino game in the USA. During the Wild West era, 'gaffed' (cheating) dealing boxes became infamous, leading to skepticism even when honest games were offered.

setup.players: Any number of players can bet against a single Banker. Traditionally 1-10 players.
setup.deck: Standard 52-card deck. Card ranks: Ace (low) through King (high).
setup.dealing: Dealer (the Banker) shuffles the deck and places it in the dealing box. The first card exposed (the 'Soda') is a dead card and is removed from play. Betting then begins.
setup.equipment: 1. **Dealing Box**: Special box with a slot to expose card faces while preventing double-dealing. 2. **Layout**: Pasteboard or cloth with 13 card ranks (Ace through King) where players place bets. 3. **Case Keeper**: An abacus-like device with beads to track which cards have been drawn from the deck. 4. **Coppers**: Hexagonal tokens placed on bets to indicate 'losing' prediction.

rules.objective: Wager on whether a specific card rank will be the next 'Winner' or 'Loser' card drawn from the dealing box.
rules.gameplay: 1. **Betting Phase**: Players place chips on any card rank on the layout, indicating a bet that card will 'Win' (be drawn as the second card in a turn). 2. **The Draw**: Dealer exposes two cards from the box in sequence. 3. **Card 1 (Loser)**: The first card is the LOSER. The House collects all bets on that rank (unless 'coppering' was used). 4. **Card 2 (Winner)**: The second card is the WINNER. The House pays 1:1 on all bets on that rank. 5. **Next Turn**: Betting resumes for the next pair of cards. The game continues until the deck is exhausted.
keyRules: **Soda**: The first card of the entire deck (removed before play begins; not part of gameplay).
**Hock**: The last card remaining in the deck (visible in the box but rarely played).
**Coppering**: A player places a hexagonal copper token on their chip to bet that a card will LOSE (be drawn first). Inverts the normal bet outcome.
**Splits**: If both cards in a draw are the same rank (e.g., two 4s), the House takes half of all bets on that rank (both winning and losing bets are halved). This is the House's sole edge.
**Calling the Turn**: When only 3 cards remain in the deck, players may bet on the exact order they will appear. This exotic bet pays 4:1 (or sometimes 3:1 depending on house rules).
**Card Exhaustion**: Once a rank has been drawn 4 times (all cards of that rank removed), no further bets on that rank are accepted.
**Even Money Bets**: Standard bets pay 1:1 on wins. No juice or commission is charged on winning bets (unique advantage vs. other gambling games).

strategy.basic: Use the Case Keeper religiously. Never bet on an 'exhausted' card (one that has all 4 remaining cards drawn). This single rule eliminates most losing propositions.
strategy.intermediate: **Split Probability**: As the deck thins, calculate the likelihood of splits. If only one 5 remains in the deck, a 5-5 split is impossibleâ€”bets on 5 become slightly favored. Conversely, if multiple cards of the same rank remain, splits become more likely, worsening odds on those ranks. **Coppering Strategy**: Copper bets on ranks where you believe a specific card is about to be drawn as the Loser first.
strategy.advanced: **Deck State Analysis**: Track not just which ranks remain but which specific suits remain. Some dealing boxes may show card orientation, hinting at suit. **Bet Sizing**: Use the Case Keeper to identify the single turning (3-card ending) opportunityâ€”this is the only time an exotic 4:1 bet becomes favorable. **Martingale Rejection**: Resist the temptation to use the Martingale system (doubling bets after losses). Faro's random nature makes all betting systems statistically unreliable long-term.
tips: The House edge comes entirely from splits. Even on an even-money game, you face a ~1.4% house edge on average due to splits.
Never play against a 'gaffed' (cheating) dealing box. Optical tricks, thumb movements, and mechanical boxes can manipulate outcomes.
If tracking becomes overwhelming, simply avoid splits by betting only on ranks with very few cards remaining.
The psychological edge: Bankers profit by inducing players to chase losses. Maintain discipline and quit when ahead.

variations.name: Stuss (Jewish Faro)
variations.description: Simplified version without a dealing box; cards drawn from hand. House advantage dramatically increases: on splits, House takes ALL bets (not just half). Popular in Jewish communities.

scoring.description: Betting outcomes determined by card draws. House profits from splits only.
scoring.winCondition: Player wins if their bet card is drawn as the 'Winner' (second card in a pair). Coppering inverts thisâ€”player wins if coppering bet card is drawn as 'Loser' (first card).

synthesis.shortDescription: The iconic frontier gambling game where players wager on card ranks drawn from a dealing box, prized for its transparency and low house edge.
